beats.title: Cleaning Up Legacy Mouse Input Calculations
beats.body: A contributor submitted changes to how mouse input is translated into in-game rotation before action flags are encoded. The PR removes unused legacy code, corrects a timing inconsistency that caused inaccurate sensitivity under unstable framerates, and widens the per-frame rotation limits to the maximum the action flag format supports.

beats.title: Authentic Feel vs. Improved Responsiveness: Where Should the Turn-Rate Ceiling Sit?
beats.body: Widening the per-frame rotation cap measurably improves quick-turn responsiveness for mouse users, but it also shifts the competitive balance in multiplayer away from keyboard players, who are already constrained by physics-model constants. The core tension is whether turn-rate limits are a correctable technical artifact or a protected part of the original game's feel and balance.

beats.title: Position A — LidMop
beats.body: The existing cap is technically inconsistent: identical physical mouse movement yields different in-game rotation depending on how it happens to be sampled across frames. LidMop initially advocated for the higher limits as a genuine improvement, but after testing conceded that the original limits are part of the gameplay and should be restored—while still wanting the sampling inconsistency fixed.
beats.author: LidMop

beats.title: Position B — treellama
beats.body: Mouse turn-rate limits are not a bug to fix but a core physics parameter that defines the game's feel and preserves decades of multiplayer balance between mouse and keyboard players. Raising the cap—even optionally via a preference slider—disadvantages keyboard players in net games and sets a precedent of treating fundamental gameplay constants as user-tunable settings.
beats.author: treellama

beats.question: Given the tension between correcting a real sampling inconsistency and preserving original multiplayer balance, what would you do with the turn-rate limits in this PR?
